q: What protected Hamza from the outbreak?
s: There is a measles outbreak at a primary school. Many children have high fevers, red eyes and a blotchy rash that started behind the ears. Hamza, 6, sits next to two of them but stays well. His records show two doses of a vaccine, at 1 year and before starting school. The sick children had missed theirs.
c: A measles outbreak, and a child with two vaccine doses who stayed well while unvaccinated children got sick.

a.w: Two doses protect against measles, mumps and rubella in about 97% of children.
It protects against TB, not measles.
It doesn't prevent measles.
It protects against flu only.

lq: Which vaccine protects against measles?

q: What treatment helped her panic attacks?
s: Mrs. Basma, 29, had sudden attacks of a racing heart, shaking and fear that she was dying, several times a week. Her heart tests were normal. She didn't want tablets. She met a therapist once a week for 12 weeks and learned to notice scary thoughts, test them and slowly face the places she avoided. Her attacks became rare.
c: Panic attacks with normal heart tests, no tablets, and weekly sessions learning to test scary thoughts and face avoided places.

a.w: CBT helps people change frightening thoughts and stop avoiding, which treats panic disorder.
It calms attacks short term but is addictive and isn't a long-term treatment.
It eases shaking but doesn't treat the fear.
Panic disorder isn't treated with surgery.

lq: What talking therapy treats panic disorder?

q: What one change helped his lungs the most?
s: Mr. Ramzy, 55, has COPD and used to smoke 30 cigarettes a day. Six months ago he used nicotine patches and a stop-smoking clinic, and he has not smoked since. His cough has eased, he is less breathless walking to the market, and his yearly lung test is falling much more slowly than before.
c: COPD, patches and a clinic, and a lung test now falling much more slowly.

a.w: It is the only thing that slows the fall in lung function in COPD.
It eases breathlessness but doesn't slow the disease.
They treat flare-ups, not the disease itself.
It helps some with very low oxygen, not the rate of decline.

lq: What is the most effective treatment for slowing COPD?

q: What helped his back the most?
s: Mr. Sameh, 38, has had low back pain for three weeks after moving furniture. There is no numbness, no leg weakness, no fever and no trouble with his bladder or bowels. His doctor told him to keep active, keep working, take simple painkillers and walk every day. In four weeks the pain was gone.
c: Simple low back pain with no warning signs, and advice to keep active and walk daily.

a.w: For simple back pain, staying active and walking speed recovery more than rest.
It slows recovery and weakens the muscles.
Not needed without warning signs, and it doesn't treat anything.
Not used for simple back pain.

lq: What is the best advice for simple low back pain?
la: Stay active, keep moving and use simple painkillers

q: What operation cured her?
s: Lina, 18, has had pain for a day that started around her belly button and moved to her lower right side. She has a fever, no appetite and vomited once. Pressing on the lower right belly hurts, and letting go hurts more. Her pregnancy test is negative. She had keyhole surgery that night and went home two days later.
c: Pain moving from the belly button to the lower right, fever, and keyhole surgery that night.

a.w: Removing the inflamed appendix cures appendicitis and stops it bursting.
Gallbladder pain is in the upper right.
A hernia is a lump, not this pain.
She isn't pregnant.

lq: What is the treatment for appendicitis?

q: What should be done first?
s: A boy of 12 cuts his forearm on broken glass in the school yard. Blood is flowing steadily from a cut about 4 cm long. There is no glass left in it that can be seen. He is pale but talking. The teacher has the first aid kit and gloves.
c: A steadily bleeding cut with no glass seen in it.

a.o: Firm direct pressure with a clean pad
a.w: Pressing firmly on the wound for at least 10 minutes is the first way to stop bleeding.
Only for life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure can't stop.

a.o: Washing it under the tap first
a.w: It wastes time while it bleeds.
Blood loss is the danger; press it.

lq: What is the first step for a bleeding cut?
la: Firm direct pressure on the wound with a clean pad

q: What treatment years ago damaged his heart?
s: Mr. Medhat, 45, had Hodgkin lymphoma at 19 and was cured. Part of his treatment was aimed at his chest every weekday for several weeks. Now he has chest pain on walking, and a scan shows narrowed heart arteries and a stiff, thickened aortic valve. He doesn't smoke, his cholesterol is normal and nobody in his family has heart disease.
t: Radiotherapy and the heart, years later
c: Treatment aimed at the chest every weekday for weeks in his teens, then early heart artery and valve disease.

a.w: Radiation to the chest can damage the heart arteries and valves decades later, so survivors need heart checks.
A test, not a treatment, and it doesn't harm the heart.
Short courses don't cause valve disease.
They don't harm the heart this way.

lq: What late heart problems can chest radiotherapy cause?
la: Early coronary artery disease and valve disease

q: Which tablet made his skin burn so easily?
s: Mr. Hazem, 23, is taking a daily tablet for acne. On a beach trip he sat in the sun for an hour, like his friends, but he came home with a painful, blistering burn on his face and arms, much worse than theirs. He never burns like this. His friends, who weren't taking anything, only went a little pink.
c: An acne tablet, and a burn after one hour in the sun far worse than his friends'.

a.w: It makes the skin very sensitive to sunlight, so sunscreen and covering up are advised.
A cream that can dry the skin, but not a tablet.
They don't make the skin burn.
It doesn't make the skin sun-sensitive.

lq: Which acne antibiotic makes the skin burn in the sun?

q: Which treatment didn't help her sore throat?
s: Rawan, 22, has had a sore throat, runny nose, hoarse voice and a mild cough for three days. She has no fever, her tonsils are red but without pus, and her neck glands are not swollen. She was given an antibiotic, took it for five days, and felt no different. On the seventh day the illness went away by itself.
t: Antibiotics for a viral sore throat
c: A sore throat with a runny nose, cough and hoarse voice, no fever, no pus, and an antibiotic that changed nothing.

a.w: A sore throat with cold symptoms and no fever is almost always viral, so antibiotics don't help.
It eases the pain and works for viral sore throats.
They soothe the throat.
They help her recover.

lq: Why don't antibiotics help most sore throats?

q: What antidote is given?
s: Mrs. Nabila, 82, takes digoxin for an irregular heartbeat. After her kidney function worsened, she became confused, vomited and saw yellow halos. Now her pulse is 32 and her potassium is 6.4. Her ECG shows a dangerous rhythm, and the level of her heart drug is very high. Atropine hasn't helped. The doctor orders vials of a special antidote.
c: Very high digoxin, a pulse of 32, high potassium and a dangerous rhythm despite atropine.

a.w: They bind digoxin in the blood and reverse its effects within an hour.
Used for high potassium, but traditionally avoided in digoxin toxicity.
It reverses opioids only.
It reverses heparin only.

lq: What is the antidote for severe digoxin toxicity?

q: Which new drug pushed her sugar so high?
s: Mrs. Thanaa, 66, has type 2 diabetes, well controlled on metformin. A week ago she was given a daily tablet for a flare of her lung disease. Since then her sugar has risen to 22 every afternoon, she is thirsty and passing a lot of urine. There are no ketones and no infection in her urine.
c: Well-controlled diabetes, a new daily tablet for a lung flare, then high afternoon sugars.

a.w: Steroids raise blood sugar, often most in the afternoon, so diabetes needs closer care while on them.
It raises sugar only a little.
It doesn't raise sugar like this.
It doesn't raise sugar.

lq: How do steroid tablets affect diabetes?
la: They raise blood sugar, often most in the afternoon

q: Which tablet should not have been given for his diarrhea?
s: Mr. Hamdi, 70, was in hospital for a chest infection and got diarrhea after antibiotics. Without testing, he was given a tablet to stop the diarrhea. Two days later he has a fever, a swollen, tender belly and very few stools, and his white count is high. His stool test now shows C. difficile toxin.
c: Diarrhea after antibiotics, a stopper tablet given before testing, then a swollen belly and C. difficile.

a.w: In C. difficile, stopping the bowel traps the toxin and can lead to a dangerously swollen colon.
The right treatment for C. difficile.
Safe and helpful in diarrhea.
It doesn't stop the bowel.

lq: Why is loperamide avoided in C. difficile diarrhea?
la: It traps the toxin and can cause a dangerously swollen colon

q: What treatment years ago affects his fertility?
s: Mr. Kareem, 30, had leukemia at 10 and was cured after two years of strong medicines through drips and tablets. He and his wife have tried for a baby for two years. His semen test shows almost no sperm. Nobody stored his sperm back then. His hormone tests show the testes are damaged, not the brain signals.
c: Two years of strong drip medicines for childhood leukemia, then almost no sperm and damaged testes.

a.w: Many chemotherapy drugs damage the testes and can leave men infertile years later. Storing sperm first is now offered.
They don't harm fertility.
They don't cause lasting infertility.
It doesn't harm sperm.

lq: Why is fertility preservation offered before chemotherapy?

q: Which stomach tablet weakened his clopidogrel?
s: Mr. Sabry, 63, had a stent put in his heart artery and takes aspirin and clopidogrel. His GP added a tablet to protect his stomach. His heart doctor quickly swaps it for a different stomach tablet, saying this one blocks the liver enzyme that switches clopidogrel on. The new one is pantoprazole.
c: Clopidogrel needs a liver enzyme to work, and one stomach tablet blocks that enzyme.

a.w: It blocks CYP2C19, the enzyme that activates clopidogrel, so clopidogrel works less. Pantoprazole affects it less.
The safer stomach tablet he was switched to.
An antacid that doesn't block the enzyme.
It doesn't block this enzyme much.

lq: Which PPI weakens clopidogrel?

q: Which antibiotic must not be mixed with calcium drips in newborns?
s: Baby Yousef, 10 days old, is in the neonatal unit with suspected sepsis and needs IV calcium for low calcium. The pharmacist stops the planned antibiotic for him and suggests cefotaxime instead. She explains that the planned one can form crystals with calcium in a newborn's lungs and kidneys, which can be fatal.
t: Ceftriaxone with calcium in a baby
c: A newborn on IV calcium, and an antibiotic that forms crystals with calcium.

a.w: In newborns it can form deadly crystals with IV calcium and also raise jaundice, so cefotaxime is used.
The safer choice suggested.
Often used in newborn sepsis, and it doesn't crystallize with calcium.
Often used in newborns, and it doesn't do this.

lq: Which antibiotic is avoided with IV calcium in newborns?

q: Which transplant drug is slowly harming his new kidney?
s: Mr. Ehab, 52, had a kidney transplant eight years ago. He takes several tablets to stop rejection, one of which has its blood level checked often. His gums have grown thick and he has more body hair than before. His pressure is high, and his kidney numbers are slowly rising. A biopsy shows scarring, but no rejection.
c: Transplant drugs, thick gums, more hair, high pressure and a slowly scarring kidney with no rejection.

a.w: It protects against rejection but can slowly scar the kidney, raise pressure, thicken gums and grow hair.
It causes weight gain and high sugar, not thick gums and kidney scarring.
It affects the blood count and gut, not the kidneys like this.
It can also thicken gums, but it doesn't scar the kidney.

lq: Which transplant drug can scar the kidney and thicken the gums?

q: What made his headaches worse?
s: Mr. Hossam, 40, has had headaches for years and takes painkillers almost every day, sometimes with codeine, to keep going. Now he has a headache 25 days a month, worse on waking. His brain scan and eye check are normal. His doctor tells him to stop the tablets, and after a hard two weeks his headaches drop to a few a month.
c: Painkillers taken almost every day, near-daily headaches, normal tests, and improvement after stopping.

a.w: Taking painkillers more than 10 to 15 days a month causes medication overuse headache. Stopping them breaks the cycle.
A migraine preventer he wasn't taking.
It wouldn't cause headaches.
His eye check is normal.

lq: What causes medication overuse headache?
la: Taking painkillers on more than 10-15 days a month

q: Which long-term tablet caused her womb lining to thicken?
s: Mrs. Nadia, 58, had breast cancer four years ago and takes a daily tablet to stop it coming back. Her periods stopped years ago, but now she has vaginal bleeding. A scan shows a thickened lining of the womb, and a biopsy finds early cancer of the womb lining. Her breast cancer has not returned.
c: A daily tablet after breast cancer, bleeding after menopause and a thickened womb lining.

a.w: It blocks estrogen in the breast but acts like estrogen in the womb, raising the risk of womb lining cancer.
It lowers estrogen everywhere and doesn't thicken the womb lining.
They protect the bones only.
It doesn't affect the womb.

lq: Which breast cancer drug raises the risk of womb cancer?

q: Which long-term tablet clouded his lenses?
s: Mr. Waleed, 48, has had a kidney transplant for 12 years and takes tablets every day to protect it, including one that makes his face round. Now his vision is foggy in both eyes, with glare from headlights at night. The eye doctor sees cloudy patches at the back of both lenses. He has no diabetes.
c: Long-term transplant tablets including one that rounds the face, and cloudy patches at the back of both lenses.

a.w: Long-term steroids cause cataracts at the back of the lens and can also raise eye pressure.
It can raise sugar and harm the kidneys, but doesn't cause cataracts.
It doesn't cause cataracts.
It doesn't affect the lens.

lq: What type of cataract do long-term steroids cause?

q: Which long-term tablet thinned her bones?
s: Mrs. Nawal, 62, has taken a daily tablet for heartburn for 10 years, never stopping. Her magnesium is low, and a bone scan shows thin bones. Last month she broke her wrist in a simple fall. c: Ten years of a daily heartburn tablet, low magnesium, thin bones and a fracture from a simple fall.

a.w: Years of PPIs lower stomach acid, which reduces calcium and magnesium absorption and raises fracture risk.
An antacid taken now and then, not linked to fractures.
It doesn't thin the bones.
It doesn't thin the bones.

la: Low magnesium, thin bones and fractures, and gut infections

a.w: It blocks the liver enzyme that clears carbamazepine, so carbamazepine can build up to toxic levels.
The safe choice she picked.
Safe with carbamazepine.
It doesn't affect carbamazepine levels.

lq: Which antibiotic raises carbamazepine levels?

q: Which treatment should she not have been given?
s: Mrs. Hayam, 26, has an eating disorder with bingeing and making herself sick, and also wants to stop smoking. Her GP gave her a tablet that helps people stop smoking. A week later she had a fit for the first time ever. Her salts are a little low from vomiting, and she has no history of epilepsy.
c: An eating disorder with vomiting, a new stop-smoking tablet, then a first fit.

a.w: It lowers the fit threshold and is avoided in eating disorders like bulimia and in epilepsy.
A safe way to stop smoking here.
Another stop-smoking tablet that doesn't carry this fit risk in bulimia.
A talking therapy, not a fit risk.

lq: Which stop-smoking drug is avoided in bulimia and epilepsy?

q: What is the main treatment?
s: A family of four was found sleepy and confused in a flat with a faulty gas heater. They all have headaches and vomited. Their oxygen reads 99% on the finger, but their blood shows a high carboxyhemoglobin. The mother is the worst, confused with a level of 30%. c: A faulty heater, headaches in the whole family, normal finger oxygen and high carboxyhemoglobin.

a.w: It pushes carbon monoxide off hemoglobin much faster. Finger oxygen readings are falsely normal in CO poisoning.
It reverses opioids, not carbon monoxide.
There is no infection.
Too slow for these levels; high-flow oxygen is needed.

lq: What is the treatment for carbon monoxide poisoning?
la: High-flow 100% oxygen (hyperbaric in some severe cases)

q: What made his gout attack last longer?
s: Mr. Fathi, 55, has his first gout attack in his big toe. His doctor gives naproxen and also starts allopurinol at a high dose the same day, to lower his uric acid fast. Instead of settling in days, the attack drags on for three weeks and spreads to his ankle. His kidney tests are normal.
c: A first gout attack and a uric acid lowering tablet started at a high dose the same day.

a.o: Starting allopurinol during the attack at a high dose
a.w: A sudden fall in uric acid can prolong or trigger attacks. It is started low and slowly, with cover.
The right drug to calm the attack.
They ease the pain.
Helps the attack settle.

lq: How should allopurinol be started?
la: At a low dose, raised slowly, often with colchicine or an NSAID as cover

q: What reversed his paralysis?
s: Mr. Ahmed, 45, had keyhole stomach surgery under general anesthesia with a muscle relaxant called rocuronium. At the end, he can't lift his head and his breathing is weak, because the relaxant is still working. The anesthetist gives an injection that wraps up the rocuronium in the blood. c: Rocuronium still working at the end of surgery, and an injection that wraps it up in the blood.

a.w: It binds rocuronium directly and reverses it within minutes.
It reverses opioids, not muscle relaxants.
It reverses benzodiazepines.
It treats malignant hyperthermia, not paralysis from relaxants.

lq: What reverses rocuronium?

q: What should be done first for the sting?
s: Hady, 9, was stung by a bee on his forearm in the garden. The small black sting is still in the skin with a little sac on top. The area is red, swollen and painful, but he is breathing normally, his lips and face aren't swollen, and he feels well otherwise. He isn't known to have allergies.
c: A bee sting left in the skin, with only local swelling and no signs of allergy.

a.w: Removing it quickly with a fingernail or card stops more venom going in. Then cool the area.
Squeezing the sac can push more venom in.
Only for anaphylaxis, which he doesn't have.
It doesn't help a bee sting.

lq: What is the first step for a bee sting?
la: Scrape the sting out sideways quickly, then cool the area

q: What should he be given first, before anything else?
s: Mr. Sabry, 58, has had crushing pain in the middle of his chest for 30 minutes, spreading to his left arm, with sweating and sickness. His ECG shows a heart attack, and the team is calling the cath lab. He has no allergies, no stomach bleeding, and he takes no blood thinners.
t: Aspirin to chew in a heart attack
c: A heart attack on the ECG, no allergy and no bleeding risk, while the cath lab is being called.

a.w: Chewed aspirin stops platelets clumping on the clot. It is given straight away in a heart attack.
It eases pain but does nothing for the clot.
Not the first step; it can drop the pressure.
A water tablet; he isn't fluid-overloaded.

lq: What is chewed straight away in a suspected heart attack?

q: Which treatment caused the extra hair fall at first?
s: Mr. Omar, 29, has thinning hair at the crown and started a lotion rubbed into his scalp twice a day. For the first six weeks, more hair fell out than before, which worried him. His doctor told him to keep going. By four months, new short hairs were growing and the thin patch looked fuller.
c: A scalp lotion twice a day, more hair fall in the first weeks, then regrowth by four months.

a.w: It pushes resting hairs out so new ones grow, so a short shed in the first weeks is normal.
It treats dandruff and doesn't regrow hair this way.
For itchy scalp conditions, not thinning hair.
They don't cause a shed or regrow hair in men like this.

lq: Why can hair fall more at first on minoxidil?
la: Resting hairs are pushed out as new growth starts

q: What cleared his blocked ear?
s: Mr. Hamed, 70, feels his left ear is blocked and his hearing on that side is muffled. The doctor sees the ear canal full of hard, dark wax, with no infection. He was told to put a few drops of something from the kitchen into that ear every night for two weeks, lying on his side for five minutes. After two weeks the wax came out and his hearing returned.
c: Hard wax blocking the canal, and a few drops from the kitchen every night for two weeks.

a.w: They soften the wax so it comes out by itself or is easy to remove.
They push wax deeper and can hurt the ear.
There is no infection.
They don't work and can burn the ear.

lq: What is the first treatment for hard ear wax?
la: Softening drops, such as olive oil, for one to two weeks

q: What should be done first?
s: On a hot summer afternoon, a construction worker, 35, collapses at a building site. His skin is hot and dry, his temperature is over 40, and he is confused and slurring his words. He has been working in the sun all day and drank little. Someone has called an ambulance.
c: Hot dry skin, a temperature over 40 and confusion after working all day in the sun.

a.w: Move him to the shade, remove extra clothes, and soak him with cool water while fanning. Fast cooling saves the brain.
It doesn't lower temperature in heat stroke.
It traps the heat.

a.o: Make him drink a lot quickly
a.w: He is confused and may choke; cooling comes first.

lq: What is the first treatment for heat stroke?
la: Rapid cooling with water and fanning

q: What should she be given now?
s: Mrs. Amira, 52, uses insulin for diabetes. She skipped lunch and is now shaky, sweaty and confused, but awake and able to swallow. Her sugar is 2.6. She has no chest pain or weakness on one side. Her husband is with her.
c: Insulin, a skipped meal, a sugar of 2.6, and she can still swallow.

a.w: 15 to 20 g of fast sugar, such as juice or glucose tablets, then recheck in 15 minutes and follow with a snack.
It would lower her sugar further.
Used when someone can't swallow safely; she can.
It is too slow to raise the sugar.

lq: What is the first step for low sugar in someone who can swallow?
la: 15-20 g fast sugar by mouth, recheck after 15 minutes

q: What eased her heartburn quickly?
s: Mrs. Basma, 35, gets a burning feeling behind her breastbone after big, spicy meals, worse when she lies down. She has no weight loss, no trouble swallowing and no vomiting blood. She chewed two chalky tablets from the pharmacy after meals, and the burning settled within minutes.
c: Burning after big spicy meals, no warning signs, and chalky tablets that worked within minutes.

a.w: They neutralize stomach acid quickly and ease heartburn within minutes.
It stops diarrhea, not heartburn.
They treat constipation.
Heartburn isn't an infection.

lq: What eases simple heartburn within minutes?

q: What helped him hear at school?
s: Ziad, 7, has a hearing loss that runs in his father's family. His hearing test shows moderate loss in both ears; his eardrums are normal with no fluid. After he was fitted with small devices behind both ears, he followed lessons well and his speech improved.
c: An inherited hearing loss with normal eardrums and small devices worn behind both ears.

a.w: They make sounds louder for moderate nerve hearing loss.
They drain fluid, which he doesn't have.
There is no infection.
There is no wax.

lq: What is used for moderate inherited nerve hearing loss in children?

q: What fixed her tingling and anemia?
s: Mrs. Soad, 60, is tired and pale, with tingling feet and a sore red tongue. Her red cells are large and her vitamin B12 is low. She has antibodies against the stomach cells that help take up B12. She now has an injection every three months for life, and her blood and feet improved.
c: Large red cells, low B12, stomach antibodies, and an injection every three months for life.

a.w: In pernicious anemia B12 can't be absorbed from food, so it is given by injection.
Iron deficiency makes small red cells, not large ones.

Not needed for a steady B12 anemia.

q: What cleared her urine infection?

c: Burning and frequent urine, no fever or back pain, and three days of tablets.

a.w: A common first antibiotic for a simple bladder infection.
For skin infections, not urine.
The infection is bacterial.
They don't treat infection.

lq: What is a common first antibiotic for simple cystitis?

q: Which new prostate tablet made him dizzy on standing?

c: A new bedtime prostate tablet, a better stream, and faintness when getting up quickly.

It doesn't affect pressure.

c: Mild sickness in early pregnancy with no dehydration, eased by small snacks and ginger.

a.w: Mild morning sickness usually eases with simple changes like these.
Needed only for severe vomiting with dehydration.
It makes sickness worse.
Morning sickness isn't an infection.

lq: What helps mild morning sickness?

Usually not needed for a simple stye.

They don't cause diarrhea.

It doesn't cause stomach bleeding.
A cream on the skin, not a cause of ulcers.

q: What fixed his lump?

A hernia isn't an infection.

q: What should be done for the nosebleed?
s: Nour, 10, has a nosebleed while doing homework. Blood drips from one nostril. She is alert, breathing well and didn't hit her head. Her mother has a tissue and a bowl. Nour wants to lie down and tip her head back.

a.o: Sit forward and pinch the soft nose

a.o: Pinch the bony top of the nose
a.w: The bleeding is from the soft front part.

s: Mr. Raouf, 50, took a whole strip of the slow-release tablets he uses for his heart rhythm. Six hours later his pulse is 38 and his pressure is 70/40. q: What daily habit is cutting his risk of another skin cancer?
s: Mr. Hany, 62, a fisherman with fair skin, had a basal cell skin cancer removed from his nose two years ago. c: A fair-skinned fisherman after a skin cancer, a hat, avoiding midday sun and a cream every two hours.

a.w: Daily high-factor sunscreen, with shade and a hat, lowers the risk of new sun-related skin cancers.
It keeps the skin soft but doesn't block UV.
They don't protect the skin.
It doesn't prevent skin cancer.

q: Which vaccine lowers the risk of this throat cancer?

c: A throat and tonsil cancer in non-smokers caused by a virus, and a vaccine at 9 to 14 that also protects the cervix.

a.w: It protects against the human papillomavirus types that cause cervical and many throat cancers.
It prevents liver cancer from hepatitis B, not throat cancer.
It protects against measles, mumps and rubella.
It protects against flu only.

lq: Which vaccine helps prevent throat and cervical cancers?

q: What antidote is given?
s: Firefighters pull Mr. Sherif, 45, from a burning house full of smoke from melting plastic furniture. He is confused, then has a fit. His blood is very acidic with a lactate of 12. His oxygen level reads normal and his carbon monoxide level is only mildly raised. The doctor gives a dark red drip that turns his skin and urine red.
c: Smoke from burning plastic, a very high lactate, normal oxygen, mild CO, and a dark red drip.

a.w: It binds cyanide from burning plastics. It turns the skin and urine red.
It reverses opioids only.
It reverses benzodiazepines.
For insecticide poisoning.

q: Why did his insulin stop working?
s: Mr. Hamdy, 35, has type 1 diabetes. He went on a summer trip and kept his insulin pen in the car's glove box all day for a week. q: What should be given for his bleeding?

c: Warfarin, an INR of 8 and a big bleed, treated with an IV vitamin and clotting factor concentrate.

a.o: Vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate
a.w: Vitamin K reverses warfarin over hours, and the factor concentrate works within minutes in a major bleed.
It reverses heparin, not warfarin.
Warfarin doesn't lower platelets.
It doesn't reverse warfarin.

q: What operation lowered her breast cancer risk the most?
s: Mrs. Marwa, 32, lost her mother and aunt to breast cancer young. A gene test showed she carries the same faulty gene, giving her a very high lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer. c: A faulty family gene with very high breast and ovarian cancer risk, and an operation on both breasts.

a.w: In BRCA carriers it lowers breast cancer risk by about 90%. Ovaries are often removed later for ovarian risk.
It removes a tumor, and she has none.
Removing the womb doesn't lower breast cancer risk.
It treats cancer; it isn't used to prevent it here.

lq: What lowers breast cancer risk most in BRCA carriers?

q: Which treatment dropped her platelets and caused a clot?

One dose wouldn't cause antibodies and clots like this.
They don't cause clots.

q: What will protect him from rabies?

c: A deep stray dog bite, washing, antibodies around the wound, and a course of injections.

It prevents tetanus, not rabies.
They treat wound infection, not rabies.
Once symptoms start, it is too late.

A blood pressure tablet that is safe in pregnancy.
Safe in pregnancy and used for diabetes.
Advised in pregnancy, especially with diabetes.

lq: Which epilepsy drug often needs a higher dose in pregnancy?

q: Why did her fertility tablets not work?

c: A woman who already releases eggs, given egg-releasing tablets, with a husband who has almost no sperm.

A good supplement, not a fertility treatment.
It doesn't cause eggs to release.

q: What should be done straight away?
s: Mr. Atef, 40, a cleaner, splashed strong drain cleaner into his right eye a minute ago. He is screaming in pain and can't open the eye. The drain cleaner is an alkali. There is a sink and an eye wash bottle nearby. His left eye is fine.

a.w: Alkalis burn deep fast. Constant washing, holding the lids open, starts at once, before going to hospital.
